commands.name: harness

commands.name: harness-resume

commands.name: harness-start

commands.name: harness-status

commands.name: harness-stop

commands.name: subagent-task-tree
commands.description: Execute a multi-task implementation plan as a chained subagent tree — you are the parent controller; you spawn one manager per task; each manager spawns a planner, a plan-auditor, one implementer per subtask, per-subtask auditors, and a final drift-auditor. (user)

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

commands.name: batch

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser

It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small, dependency-free Python tool, **pennywise**, that parses the ledger and reports where the money went — usable both as an importable library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python ≥3.9 package `pennywise` (src layout, `pyproject.toml` with setuptools, `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`) so that `pip install .` provides both the library and the console command. It has three parts:

1. **Ledger core** — `Entry` model, `parse(text)`, `ParseError`.
2. **Reports** — `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`.
3. **CLI** — `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export` subcommands with `--json`, stdin (`-`) support and the specified exit codes.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I can `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries in file order, each with `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`decimal.Decimal`), `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent).
2. As a user, a bad line in my ledger raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError` subclass) with `.line` = 1-based line number (blank and comment lines counted) and a message containing `line N`.
3. As a user, I can compute `balance(entries)` (Decimal, `0` for none), `by_category(entries)` and `by_month(entries)` (dicts of key → Decimal total; month key `"YYYY-MM"`).
4. As a user, I can `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` — case-insensitive category, inclusive date bounds, `None` = not filtered, order preserved.
5. As a user, `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals.
6. As a user, `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one `NAME  TOTAL` line per group, sorted by name (default `--by category`).
7. As a user, `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints matching entries oldest first (stable for same day) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.
8. As a user, `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends a normalised entry (creating the file if needed), prints the line added, and refuses invalid entries leaving the file byte-for-byte unchanged.
9. As a user, `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
10. As a user, `balance`, `summary`, `list` accept `--json`.
11. As a user, `-` as FILE reads stdin for every reading command.
12. As a user, exit codes are 0 success / 1 ledger or add-entry mistake (stderr names the line, stdout empty) / 2 unreadable file or bad command line.

## Implementation Decisions

Decisions taken on ambiguous points (the brief below stays the top authority):

- **Layout**: `pyproject.toml` (setuptools backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies), `src/pennywise/__init__.py` (re-exports `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`), `src/pennywise/ledger.py` (model + parser + formatting helper), `src/pennywise/reports.py` (aggregations/filter), `src/pennywise/cli.py` (`main(argv=None) -> int`), `src/pennywise/__main__.py` (so `python -m pennywise` works). Tests in `tests/` using stdlib `unittest` only (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`).
- **Entry**: a frozen `@dataclass` `Entry(date, category, amount, note="")`.
- **Line grammar**: strip trailing `\r`/`\n`. A line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment. Otherwise split on runs of spaces/tabs into at most 4 parts after stripping the line: `date`, `category`, `amount`, rest = note (rest of line verbatim, trimmed at both ends). Fewer than 3 fields → error.
- **Date**: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` → error).
- **Amount**: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12.`, `.5`, `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` are errors); stored as `Decimal` of that text.
- **Category**: any non-whitespace token, stored lower-cased.
- **Money formatting** (everywhere amounts are printed): quantize to `0.01`; never print negative zero (`-0.00` → `0.00`).
- **Ordering for list/export**: stable sort by date (file order kept within a day).
- **summary text format**: `f"{name}  {total}"` (two spaces), sorted by key. Empty ledger → no output. `--json` → object with sorted keys, amount strings. `--by` choices `category|month`; other values → exit 2.
- **JSON**: `balance` → `{"balance": "X.XX"}`; `list` → array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` objects (note `""` if none). Use `json.dumps` default separators, one document followed by a newline.
- **CSV**: stdlib `csv` writer with `lineterminator="\n"`; amount with two decimals; empty note → empty field. `--format` choices: `csv` only (others → exit 2). `export` has no `--json`.
- **CLI dates** (`--since`, `--until`): invalid → argparse error, exit 2.
- **add**: DATE/CATEGORY/AMOUNT/NOTE are validated with the same rules as the parser (category must be a single non-empty token with no whitespace; note must not contain a newline; note is trimmed and omitted if empty). Any invalid field → exit 1, stderr message `pennywise: line N: …` where N is the line number the entry would have taken (existing line count + 1), stdout empty, file not created/modified. The line written is the canonical `list` form (`DATE category AMOUNT.XX[ NOTE]`); if the existing file is non-empty and does not end with a newline, a newline is written first. `add` does not re-validate the existing file content. `add` does not accept `-`. - **Errors**: all error messages go to stderr prefixed `pennywise: `; ledger errors use the ParseError message, which contains `line N`. Missing/unreadable file → exit 2. No command / unknown command / bad option → exit 2 (argparse default behaviour; ensure no-subcommand also exits 2).
- **Encoding**: read/write files as UTF-8; stdin read via `sys.stdin`.

## Testing Decisions

- stdlib `unittest` only; tests in `tests/`. Library tests call functions directly; CLI tests call `pennywise.cli.main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr (and patched stdin) and assert exit code + exact output; at least one smoke test runs `python -m pennywise` as a subprocess.
- Cover every acceptance criterion below, including the brief's literal examples (the 4-line ledger → balance `1457.50`, the summary and list outputs).
- Packaging verified by `pip install .` into a fresh venv and running `pennywise balance` on the example ledger.

## Out of Scope

- Any third-party dependency; formats other than CSV for export; editing/deleting entries; currencies; budgets; config files.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` (Python ≥3.9, no third-party deps) installs an importable `pennywise` package and a `pennywise` console command.
- [ ] `parse` returns entries in order with correct `.date`/`.category` (lower-case)/`.amount` (Decimal)/`.note` (trimmed rest of line, may contain spaces, `""` if none); fields separated by any run of spaces/tabs.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00` equal; `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99` accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` rejected.
- [ ] Blank lines and `#` comment lines ignored; line numbers count them.
- [ ] Bad lines (incl. impossible dates like `2024-02-30`) raise `ParseError` (subclass of `ValueError`) with `.line` and `line N` in the message.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 for empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"` keys) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive since/until, `None` = no filter, order preserved) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the two-decimal total (`1457.50` for the brief's example).
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines; default category.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category] [--since] [--until]` prints oldest first, stable within a day, `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`, two-decimal amount.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the canonical line; invalid entry → exit 1 and file unchanged.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on `balance`, `summary`, `list` with two-decimal string amounts in the specified shapes.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `export`.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 ok; 1 ledger/add-entry mistake with stderr naming the line and empty stdout; 2 unreadable file or bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, bad `--since`/`--until` date).

## Original request
